drills.q: In one sentence, what's the key difference between stemming and lemmatization?
drills.a: Stemming chops affixes by fixed rule with no dictionary and can produce non-words; lemmatization maps to a real dictionary base form using part-of-speech and is slower.

drills.q: Why does 'saw' not stem toward 'see' even though they're the same verb?
drills.a: Stemming works by chopping shared surface affix patterns; 'saw' and 'see' share no common substring for a rule to exploit. Only a lemmatizer with dictionary/POS knowledge can resolve irregular forms like this.

drills.q: A search for the phrase 'The Who' returns results about the interrogative word 'who' instead of the band. What preprocessing step likely caused this, and why?
drills.a: Stopword removal stripped 'the' from the query, changing 'The Who' into just 'Who' — an entirely different, more common query with different correct results.

drills.q: Derive why a term appearing in every document of a corpus contributes zero to a TF-IDF score.
drills.a: IDF(t) = log(N/df(t)). If the term appears in every document, df(t) = N, so IDF = log(1) = 0, and TF-IDF = TF * 0 = 0 regardless of term frequency.

drills.q: BM25 with b=0 behaves differently than with b=0.75. Explain the difference and which is likely misconfigured.
drills.a: b controls length normalization; b=0 disables it entirely, so long documents score higher purely by having more chances to contain query terms, regardless of relevance. b=0.75 is the standard default balancing saturation against over-penalizing legitimately long documents. b=0 in a general-purpose search system is usually a misconfiguration.

drills.q: A colleague proposes stemming all documents before feeding them to a BGE embedding model to 'normalize' the text. What's wrong with this plan?
drills.a: The embedding model was trained on natural, unstemmed text; feeding it stemmed non-words (e.g. 'univers' instead of 'universal') produces token sequences it never saw in training, degrading embedding quality silently since it still returns a vector, just a worse one.

drills.q: Two documents contain visually identical text but one uses NFC-normalized Unicode and the other NFD. A user's query matches one but not the other. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: NFC vs NFD represent the same visual character with different byte sequences (precomposed codepoint vs base character + combining mark), so exact-match/hashing treats them as different strings. Fix: normalize all text to NFC (or NFKC) at ingestion, applied consistently to both the query and document indexing paths.

drills.q: Your product serves 22 locales and relies on a stem-then-BM25 pipeline for lexical search. What's the specific production risk, and what's the mitigation?
drills.a: Stemmers exist as high-quality resources for only a few dozen languages; many locales have no maintained stemmer at all, so retrieval quality is silently uneven across languages until a locale-specific bug surfaces. Mitigation: push morphological normalization onto the dense embedding leg (which learns cross-lingual structure from data) and restrict BM25's job to exact-token matching rather than linguistically correct stemming in every locale.

drills.q: A SKU code like 'iOS17-PRO' gets mangled by a stemmer before indexing and users can no longer find it by exact search. What's the fix?
drills.a: Exclude exact identifiers (SKUs, version strings, error codes) from stemming entirely — stemming rules apply uniformly by surface pattern with no awareness of identifier semantics, so the lexical leg needs an identifier-detection step (or simply skip stemming for the BM25 leg) to preserve exact matches for this class of term.

drills.q: Ingested documents from a legacy CMS show up in your search index with garbled characters like 'Ã©' instead of 'é'. Diagnose and fix.
drills.a: This is mojibake — text decoded with the wrong character encoding upstream. It degrades both the lexical index (garbage terms matching nothing) and embeddings (vectors for noise). Fix by enforcing UTF-8 end-to-end and correcting the decode step at ingestion; downstream patching is unreliable since the original bytes may already be unrecoverable.

drills.q: When is a full classical preprocessing pipeline (stem, stopword removal, lowercase) still the right choice in production?
drills.a: For a pure BM25/lexical-only system with no dense embedding leg — log search, code search, structured lookup — where exact-term matching dominates, a mature stemmer exists for the languages involved, and the latency/cost budget can't support an embedding model.
